opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we think about a lot, because when you see an impressive result you always have to ask: how much of this is the model, and how much is the harness around it?

Scaffolding matters, but probably less than people sometimes assume, and in a somewhat different way. Hand-crafted scaffolding, with elaborate prompting chains, task-specific tools, and carefully designed workflows, can give you a real boost on a particular benchmark. But those gains often don't transfer well. You can overfit the scaffold to the task distribution just like you can overfit a model. So when a result depends heavily on very bespoke engineering, I discount it somewhat as a signal about general capability.

On the other hand, I think it's a mistake to evaluate models with no scaffolding at all and call that their capability. In the real world, people will put these models in agent loops, give them tools, let them run code, retry, and use more compute at inference time. If you're trying to answer "what could this system actually do if someone deployed it or misused it?", you want something close to a reasonable best effort at elicitation. Otherwise you systematically underestimate risk. The failure mode we worry about most from a safety perspective is a lab running a weak eval, concluding the model can't do something dangerous, and then six months later someone with a better harness shows that it can.

So the way I'd frame it is that we care about the gap between what you see with fairly basic, general scaffolding and what you could get with serious elicitation effort. If that gap is small, great, your measurements are robust. If it's large, or you haven't really tried to measure it, you should be pretty uncertain about any capability claim.

One trend that's been interesting is that as models get better, the marginal value of clever scaffolding seems to shrink. A lot of what scaffolds used to provide, like planning, self-correction, and breaking tasks into steps, models increasingly do on their own if you just give them a simple loop, some tools, and enough tokens. The things that still matter a lot are the basics: does the agent have the right tools, can it see its errors, does it have enough time and compute budget, and is the environment set up so it isn't failing for silly reasons? A surprising fraction of apparent "capability failures" are really the model getting tripped up by some environment quirk a human would also struggle with if they had the same interface.

So when I look at an impressive headline result, my questions are roughly these. How general is the scaffold? How much was it tuned on the test tasks? How much compute was spent per attempt, and is the comparison to humans fair on that front? And does the result hold up across a broader task distribution, or is it a cherry-picked slice? Those tell you much more than the headline number does.

r001.rationale: It says elaborate, task-specific scaffolding can boost a particular benchmark, while those gains often do not transfer well.

r002.rationale: It describes gains that fail to transfer and possible overfitting, but does not clearly state that performance on other tasks may worsen.

r003.rationale: It says to examine how much the scaffold was tuned on the test tasks.

r004.rationale: It says clever scaffolding’s marginal value seems to shrink as models improve, but does not state that elaborate scaffolding generally performs little better than a basic harness.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think scaffolding is one of the most underappreciated and also most misunderstood variables when people try to interpret headline results.

The first thing I'd say is that scaffolding is not a confound you can subtract out. It's part of the system. When we run evaluations at METR, what we're actually measuring is "model plus agent harness plus tools plus prompting," and the gap between a naive setup and a well-engineered one can be enormous. We've seen cases where moving from a basic loop to something with better tool handling, context management, and the ability to recover from errors turns a model that looks like it can't do a task into one that completes it reliably. So if someone shows you a number, the first question should be: what was the scaffold, how much effort went into it, and was it tuned on this task distribution?

That cuts both ways, though. Weak scaffolding leads people to underestimate capabilities, and I actually think that's the more dangerous direction from a safety perspective. If you run an undertrained harness and conclude the model can't do something, you've learned very little, because a motivated actor, or the model itself in a more agentic setting, could get much more out of it. Our elicitation work is largely about not being fooled in that direction. We want a reasonably good-faith attempt to get the most out of the model, so the result approximates what's actually achievable rather than what a lazy baseline shows.

The second thing is that scaffolding effects tend to shrink in relative importance as models get stronger. A lot of what early scaffolds did was compensate for the model: parsing its outputs, forcing structure, retrying when it got confused. Frontier models increasingly handle that themselves, and labs are training them on agentic trajectories directly, so the "scaffold" is being absorbed into the model. That means a result from a heavily engineered 2023 harness and a result from a nearly bare 2025 model aren't comparable even if the numbers look similar. It also means that when someone claims a big jump purely from a clever scaffold, I'm a bit skeptical that it generalizes beyond the benchmark they tuned it on.

Third, there's a question of what you're trying to learn. If you want to know "can this system, as deployed, do dangerous things autonomously," then you should evaluate the deployed configuration and also something more aggressive, because adversaries will improve on it. If you want to know "what are the underlying capabilities of the weights," scaffolding is noise you'd like to bound. We try to report things like how task success scales with compute budget and attempts, because a single pass-or-fail number hides how much the scaffold and the sampling strategy are doing.

So, practically: I treat impressive results as real but conditional. Real, because the capability was demonstrated and that's informative about what's possible. Conditional, because the number is a function of the entire setup, and the honest comparison is between systems, not models. And when the scaffold isn't described in enough detail to reproduce, I discount the result pretty heavily, not because I think people are cheating, but because the variance from harness choices alone is large enough to explain a lot of what gets reported as progress.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether the scaffold was tuned on the task distribution and questions whether benchmark gains generalize, but does not state that scaffolding yields larger improvements on narrow than diverse distributions.

r002.rationale: It expresses skepticism about generalization beyond a tuned benchmark, but does not state that narrow-task optimization may worsen performance on other tasks.

r003.rationale: It says to ask how much effort went into the scaffold and whether it was tuned on the task distribution.

r004.rationale: The response says the gap between a basic loop and a better-engineered scaffold can be enormous, rather than saying elaborate scaffolding generally adds little over a basic harness.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s important to distinguish what the model can do in a single response from what a whole system built around it can do. Scaffolding can make a big difference: giving the model tools, letting it try things and get feedback, keeping track of what it’s done, and giving it more time to work on a problem.

That doesn’t make the result unreal. We care about what people can actually accomplish with these systems. But it does affect what you can infer from an impressive demonstration. How much of the strategy was supplied by the people building the scaffold? How much was tailored to this particular task? Does it work reliably on new tasks, or are we seeing one successful run out of many?

So I’d want comparisons with simpler scaffolds, a clear account of the resources and human help involved, and results across repeated attempts. The interesting question is how much scaffolding helps the model use capabilities it already has, and how much it supplies structure that the model couldn’t generate for itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task-tailoring but does not state that optimizing scaffolding for a narrow distribution yields larger improvements than for a diverse one.

r002.rationale: It asks whether a scaffold works reliably on new tasks, but does not state that narrow-task optimization may worsen performance elsewhere.

r003.rationale: It asks how much strategy was supplied and whether the scaffold was tailored to the task, but does not identify the amount of task-specific iteration as a factor.

r004.rationale: The response recommends comparing with simpler scaffolds, but does not claim elaborate scaffolding has generally performed little better than a basic harness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s important to distinguish what the model can do on its own from what the whole system can do. A scaffold might give it tools, break a task into steps, let it try things repeatedly, or provide feedback. Those can make a substantial difference to the result.

That doesn’t make the result less real. If we’re interested in what people can accomplish with AI, the whole system is relevant. But if we’re trying to understand why a particular result is impressive, we need to know how much task-specific engineering went into it, how many attempts it took, and what help it received along the way.

I’d particularly want to see whether the same scaffold works across unfamiliar tasks. A strong result with a general scaffold tells us something different from a strong result where someone has spent a lot of time tailoring the setup to that particular problem.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a general scaffold with one tailored to a particular problem, but does not state that scaffolding yields larger improvements on a narrow task distribution than on a diverse one.

r002.rationale: It does not say that optimizing a scaffold for narrow tasks can worsen performance on other tasks.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says to examine how much task-specific engineering went into the result and how many attempts it took.

r004.rationale: It does not compare elaborate scaffolding with a basic agent harness or say that elaborate scaffolding generally performs little better.
